title: Choose input classes from the contract
summary: Use the promised behaviour to choose different kinds of input, even when the method body is hidden.
goals: Partition a method’s inputs by the behaviour promised for them.
Pair every selected input with a precise expected result.
Explain why a test is black-box and what it can reveal.
setup: You can already write an assertion. The next decision is which call deserves an assertion. Black-box testing chooses cases from a public contract: parameters, documented behaviour and observable results. You do not need to read the implementation. An equivalence class groups inputs expected to follow the same rule. Testing a representative is useful evidence, not a guarantee about every member.

worked.title: Test three different rules for a delivery charge
worked.intro:
Assume Delivery.charge(int items) is a public static method with this complete contract. Its implementation is hidden. The test class goes in a separate file in the same package.

/** Returns -1 for a negative item count.
 * Returns 0 for zero items.
 * Returns 5 for every positive item count. */
public static int charge(int items)
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class DeliveryTest {
    @Test void negativeCount_returnsMinusOne() {
        assertEquals(-1, Delivery.charge(-3));
    }
    @Test void zeroCount_isFree() {
        assertEquals(0, Delivery.charge(0));
    }
    @Test void positiveCount_hasFlatCharge() {
        assertEquals(5, Delivery.charge(8));
    }
}

steps.title: Check what can be passed
steps.html: The parameter is int. Negative integers, zero and positive integers compile. null and "8" do not fit this signature. A negative number is type-correct even when a contract treats it as an invalid business value.

steps.title: Split by the promised rule
steps.html:
Input classRepresentativeExpected
items < 0-3-1
items = 000
items > 085

The expected result comes from the comment. It is not copied from whatever the current implementation happens to return.

steps.title: Make each observation executable
steps.html: Each method makes one target call and checks the returned integer with assertEquals(expected, actual). Test names explain the situation and outcome. Separate methods make failures easy to locate.

steps.title: Justify the selection
steps.html: These are black-box cases because their selection came from the three documented rules. Choosing 8, 9 and 10 alone would repeatedly exercise the positive class while leaving the other rules unchecked.

sections.title: A complete case has an oracle
sections.html: An oracle is the basis for deciding whether the observed result is right. “Pass a negative number” is only a scenario. “Pass -3 and expect -1 because the contract rejects negative counts with -1” is a checkable case. If the contract says nothing about an input, record that uncertainty instead of inventing a promised result.

sections.title: Classes depend on behaviour, not just Java types
sections.html: A single String parameter might have null, empty, blank and nonblank classes. A count might have negative, zero and positive classes. Another contract might treat all nonpositive counts identically. Read the actual rules before deciding how to group values. Several values from one class can still be useful when they expose different boundaries or risks; the class is a starting point.

sections.title: Black-box and white-box describe the reason
sections.html:
The same input can be justified in more than one way. Selecting zero because the contract treats zero specially is black-box reasoning. Selecting zero to exercise a particular branch seen in the body is white-box reasoning. State your selection basis rather than guessing a label from the assertion name.

Grey-box testing uses partial internal knowledge along with the public contract—for example, knowing a collection keeps a cached size without having its complete source. State what information guided the case. None of these labels changes the required Java types or assertion syntax.

practice.title: Choose a useful set
practice.prompt: public static int sign(int n) promises -1 for negative values, 0 for zero, and 1 for positive values. Which set represents all documented classes?

options.feedback: These cover the negative, zero and positive rules with correct expected results.
All three calls are in the positive class; zero and negatives remain unchecked.
Neither argument fits an int parameter, so these are not runnable cases for this signature.

practice.hint: List the distinct rules before choosing values.
practice.solution: Choose -4, 0 and 7 with expected results -1, 0 and 1.

practice.title: Recognize justified claims
practice.prompt: You designed a test solely from a method’s signature and Javadoc. Select every justified statement.

options.text: The test can be classified as black-box.
options.feedback: The selection used public behaviour, without relying on internal paths.

options.text: Passing this test proves that the entire method is correct.
options.feedback: One passing case checks one observation; other inputs and faults remain possible.

options.text: The expected result needs a basis in the contract.
options.feedback: Otherwise the test may assert an invented requirement.

options.text: An invalid business value always causes a compilation error.
options.feedback: A value can fit the Java type while violating a documented restriction.

practice.hint: Separate the test’s design basis from what a passing run proves.
practice.solution: The black-box classification and contract-based expected result are justified.

practice.title: Build a test table
practice.prompt: The hidden API is public static int rebate(int price). It returns -1 for a negative price, 0 for prices 0 through 99, and 10 for prices 100 or greater. Write one representative case per class. Include input, expected result and reason.
practice.hint: There are three return rules. Do not replace an input value with a type name.
practice.solution:
InputExpectedReason
-5-1Negative price
400Price in 0–99
15010Price at least 100
rubric: Three documented classes represented.
Each row has a concrete int input and an expected int result.
Reasons quote or paraphrase the appropriate rule.

practice.title: Write the tests independently
practice.prompt:
Assume Names provides the public static method boolean isPresent(String text), which returns false for null or the empty string and true for any other string, including spaces. Write three separate JUnit 5 test methods for null, empty and nonempty inputs. Explain the classification. Assume the standard Test and Assertions imports.

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: A nullable reference still needs a specified result; a boolean result is checked with assertTrue or assertFalse.
practice.solution:
@Test void nullText_isNotPresent() {
    assertFalse(Names.isPresent(null));
}
@Test void emptyText_isNotPresent() {
    assertFalse(Names.isPresent(""));
}
@Test void nonemptyText_isPresent() {
    assertTrue(Names.isPresent("Ada"));
}

All three are black-box: the contract selected the inputs and outcomes. A space-only string is a useful additional case with expected true.
rubric: Three valid nonprivate void @Test methods.
Null and empty expect false; nonempty expects true.
Explains that case selection came from the contract.

teachBack.prompt: Why is “test an integer” less useful than “test -3 and expect -1”?
teachBack.answer: The type only tells you what kind of argument can compile. A concrete value and expected result identify the behaviour being checked.

bridge: Classes tell you where behaviour differs. Next, test the exact places where one class meets another.

title: Test boundaries and shapes
summary: Choose values just below, on and just above a limit, and separate row boundaries from column boundaries.
goals: Derive boundary cases from inclusive and exclusive limits.
Choose non-square shapes that reveal row/column confusion.
Keep every other parameter valid while targeting one boundary.
setup: An implementation can handle an ordinary value correctly but get a boundary wrong. Boundary-value testing concentrates on the edges of an input class. For integer limits, “just below” and “just above” usually mean subtracting or adding one. For an array index, the last valid position is one less than its length.

worked.title: Separate the two dimensions of a grid
worked.intro:
Assume an existing Grid class provides Grid(int rows, int columns) and the documented query below. The positive dimensions are fixed when constructed. The body of contains is hidden.

/** Returns true exactly when
 * 0 <= row < rows AND 0 <= column < columns. */
public boolean contains(int row, int column)
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class GridTest {
    @Test void lastColumn_inNonSquareGrid_isValid() {
        Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
        assertTrue(grid.contains(1, 3));
    }
    @Test void rowEqualToRowCount_isInvalid() {
        Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
        assertFalse(grid.contains(2, 1));
    }
    @Test void columnEqualToColumnCount_isInvalid() {
        Grid grid = new Grid(2, 4);
        assertFalse(grid.contains(1, 4));
    }
}

steps.title: Write each range separately
steps.html: A 2 × 4 grid has valid rows 0 and 1, and valid columns 0 through 3. The row count is not the final row index. The column count is not the final column index.

steps.title: Choose a boundary family
steps.html:
TargetValuesOther argument
Row-1, 0, 1, 2column = 1
Column-1, 0, 3, 4row = 1

Each family includes below the lower bound, the first valid index, the last valid index and the first index beyond the upper bound.

steps.title: Make a swapped dimension observable
steps.html: In a square 3 × 3 grid, confusing the two counts may produce the same answer. In a 2 × 4 grid, column 3 is valid even though 3 is not less than the row count. The first test exposes an implementation that incorrectly applies the row limit to columns.

steps.title: Target one condition at a time
steps.html: When checking row 2, column 1 is valid. When checking column 4, row 1 is valid. A call with both indexes invalid cannot tell you which boundary was enforced.

sections.title: Inclusive ranges need both sides
sections.html: For a contract accepting integers from 10 through 20 inclusive, start with 9, 10, 11 and 19, 20, 21. An ordinary interior value such as 15 adds a normal case. If the range were 10 ≤ x < 20, the top valid value would be 19. Translate the words or symbols before writing the assertion.

sections.title: Length and contents are separate dimensions
sections.html: For a sequence, consider length 0, length 1 and several elements. Then vary relevant contents. For a rectangular table, consider one row, one column and unequal row/column counts. A Java int[][] can also contain rows with different lengths or null rows. Only expect particular behaviour for those shapes if the API specifies it.

sections.title: Boundaries are selected, not guessed
sections.html: There is no universal list that makes every method thoroughly tested. A maximum integer may matter for overflow, but not every small range method needs it to demonstrate its main boundaries. Choose cases because they challenge a stated rule or plausible defect, and explain that purpose.

practice.title: Find the upper boundary
practice.prompt: boolean allowed(int n) returns true for 3 <= n && n < 8. Which expected results correctly probe the top edge?

options.feedback: Seven is the last valid integer; the strict upper limit excludes eight.
This treats an exclusive upper limit as inclusive.
These are ordinary valid cases and do not probe the upper edge.

practice.hint: Read the operator beside the upper bound.
practice.solution: The top-edge pair is 7 → true and 8 → false.

practice.title: Expose a dimension mix-up
practice.prompt: A Grid object has 2 rows and 5 columns. Its method boolean contains(int row,int column) returns true exactly when both indexes are valid: rows 0–1 and columns 0–4. Select every call whose expected result is true.

options.feedback: Row 1 and column 4 are the last valid indexes.
Row 2 equals the row count and lies outside the grid.
The first row and first column are valid.
Column 5 equals the column count and is invalid.

practice.hint: Rows range from 0 to 1; columns from 0 to 4.
practice.solution: The valid calls are (1,4) and (0,0).

practice.title: Repair a weak boundary plan
practice.prompt: Limits provides a static method boolean accepts(int n) that returns true for integers 1 through 100 inclusive and false otherwise. A proposed suite checks only 30 and 70. Replace it with a compact boundary table and explain what the original misses.
practice.hint: Write values on both sides of each inclusive endpoint.
practice.solution:

1true
2true
99true
100true

The original checks only the interior. It may miss using > instead of >= at 1 or < instead of <= at 100. A smaller four-case set 0,1,100,101 is also a justified endpoint-focused answer.
rubric: Both endpoints included as valid.
At least one immediately invalid value on each side.
Explains the boundary defect the original interior cases could miss.

practice.title: Write non-square tests
practice.prompt:
Assume a class Grid has constructor Grid(int rows, int columns) and method boolean contains(int row,int column) with valid indexes starting at zero and ending before each dimension. Write three JUnit methods for a 3 × 1 grid: last valid row, first invalid row, first invalid column. Imports are supplied.

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: A 3 × 1 grid has only column zero.
practice.solution:
@Test void lastRow_isValid() {
    Grid grid = new Grid(3, 1);
    assertTrue(grid.contains(2, 0));
}
@Test void rowAtCount_isInvalid() {
    Grid grid = new Grid(3, 1);
    assertFalse(grid.contains(3, 0));
}
@Test void columnAtCount_isInvalid() {
    Grid grid = new Grid(3, 1);
    assertFalse(grid.contains(1, 1));
}
rubric: Constructs a 3 × 1 grid.
Uses (2,0) as valid and row 3/column 1 as invalid.
Keeps the other coordinate valid for each invalid case.

teachBack.prompt: Why can ten tests on square grids miss a bug that one non-square test exposes?
teachBack.answer: Equal dimensions can hide an incorrect use of the row count where the column count belongs. Unequal dimensions make that mistake affect observable behaviour.

bridge: Now apply the same discipline to references: a missing object, an empty object and an object containing a missing field are different cases.

title: Distinguish null, empty and malformed objects
summary: Choose references that compile, then ask which values the contract accepts and what should happen for each.
goals: Distinguish null references, empty values and null fields.
Match concrete arguments to String, array and object parameters.
Avoid inventing behaviour for unspecified inputs.
setup: null means that a reference does not refer to an object. "" is an existing String with length zero. new int[0] is an existing array with no elements. An object whose field is null is still an object. These distinctions matter because the contract can assign different outcomes to each.

worked.title: Read a name contract without treating all empty-looking values alike
worked.intro:
Assume a public class NameRules has the following static method. Its implementation is hidden. Spaces are significant; this method does not trim them.

/** Returns 0 for null.
 * Otherwise returns the number of characters in text. */
public static int lengthOrZero(String text)
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class NameRulesTest {
    @Test void nullName_hasLengthZero() {
        assertEquals(0, NameRules.lengthOrZero(null));
    }
    @Test void emptyName_hasLengthZero() {
        assertEquals(0, NameRules.lengthOrZero(""));
    }
    @Test void spaces_areCounted() {
        assertEquals(3, NameRules.lengthOrZero("   "));
    }
}

steps.title: Check the argument type
steps.html: String is a reference type. A string literal and null fit this signature. The integer 3 does not become a String merely because the method can count characters.

steps.title: Separate shape from policy
steps.html: Null and empty are structurally different even though this contract returns zero for both. A white-space-only string has three characters here. Do not add a trimming requirement that is absent from the comment.

steps.title: Use a concrete expected value
steps.html: The space test expects 3. An assertion that the answer is “nonnegative” would be weaker: an incorrect answer of 0 would still pass it.

steps.title: Explain why null is legal here
steps.html: Passing null compiles, and this contract explicitly accepts it with result zero. Null should not automatically be assigned an exception expectation. The promise determines the outcome.

sections.title: A reference and its fields are different levels
sections.html:
In this small class, name is a field stored in each Contact. this means the current Contact object, so this.name = name; assigns the constructor argument on the right to that object’s field on the left. final means the field cannot be reassigned after its initialization; it does not make every object reached through a field immutable.

class Contact {
    final String name;
    Contact(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

These next declarations go inside a method, such as a test method; they are not additional top-level class declarations.

Contact absent = null;
Contact unnamed = new Contact(null);
Contact emptyName = new Contact("");

absent has no Contact object. unnamed is a Contact whose name is null. emptyName contains a real, empty String. If an API takes Contact, passing "Ada" alone is the wrong type. Construct the object first.

sections.title: Use a two-question check
sections.html:
QuestionExampleConsequence
Does the call compile?count(new int[0]) when count takes int[]The argument type fits.
Does the value satisfy the contract?An empty array when nonempty is requiredRead the stated rejection policy or record unspecified behaviour.

A method documented only for nonempty arrays does not automatically promise zero, null or an exception for an empty array. A robustness experiment may be useful, but do not report a contract violation without a relevant requirement.

sections.title: Array shape and element values
sections.html: For String[], distinguish null array, zero-length array, a one-element array containing null, and a one-element array containing "". For int[], individual elements cannot be null. These differences change both which cases compile and which behaviours they challenge.

practice.title: Select type-correct calls
practice.prompt: The only overload is public static int count(String[] values). Which arguments are type-correct? This question asks about compilation, not the method’s runtime policy.

options.feedback: String[] is a reference type; a null reference can be passed.
This is an empty String array.
A String array may contain a null reference.
One String is not a String array.
An int array is not a String array.

practice.hint: Match the declared array type before considering its contents.
practice.solution: The null reference and both String-array expressions fit. A single String and an int array do not.

practice.title: Read the promise
practice.prompt: A comment for int sum(int[] values) says “Requires a non-null array with at least one element; returns its sum.” It says nothing else about rejected inputs. What can you conclude about sum(null)?

options.text: It is type-correct, but the contract does not specify an outcome for it.
options.feedback: Null fits the reference type while violating the stated precondition.
The comment does not define that result.

options.text: It cannot compile because arrays reject null.
options.feedback: An array variable is a reference and can contain null.
No particular exception is promised.

practice.hint: Separate a precondition from an explicit rejection rule.
practice.solution: The call can compile, but no expected result for null is justified by this contract.

practice.title: Construct the right objects
practice.prompt:
Using the Contact(String name) constructor shown below, write values for: no Contact, a Contact with no name reference, an empty name, and a nonempty name. For each value, say whether it can compile as the argument to a method declared void remove(Contact contact). No removal behaviour is specified here.

class Contact {
    final String name;
    Contact(String name) { this.name = name; }
}
practice.hint: Only one case has no Contact object at all.
practice.solution:
Contact absent = null;
Contact unnamed = new Contact(null);
Contact empty = new Contact("");
Contact named = new Contact("Ada");

Each variable has type Contact, so each can be an argument to remove. Whether each input is permitted, and its expected removal result, must come from remove’s contract.
rubric: Four distinct Contact references constructed correctly.
Explains null object versus null field.
Does not invent removal outcomes without a contract.

practice.title: Design concrete reference cases
practice.prompt:
Assume Tags provides the static method int count(String[] tags), which returns 0 for a null array; otherwise counts elements that are non-null and nonempty. Spaces count as nonempty. Write four input/expected pairs covering null array, empty array, null element, and a mix of values. Then write one full @Test method for the mixed case. Imports are supplied.

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: The array exists even if one of its elements is null.
practice.solution:
InputExpected
null0

new String[]{null}0
new String[]{null, "", " ", "red"}2
@Test void mixedTags_countOnlyPresentValues() {
    String[] tags = new String[]{null, "", " ", "red"};
    assertEquals(2, Tags.count(tags));
}
rubric: Distinguishes null array, empty array and null element.
Counts a space as a nonempty string under this contract.
Uses a String[] argument and assertEquals with expected 2.

teachBack.prompt: Why is a null field not automatically a reason to expect the same behaviour as a null argument?
teachBack.answer: They are different states. A method may handle a missing object specially, then apply separate rules to fields of an existing object. Its contract determines the required outcomes.

bridge: Some methods depend on the object’s history as well as their immediate arguments. Next, test operations and state together.

title: Test an abstract data type through its operations
summary: Describe what a collection does, then test the state changes and operation sequences that define it.
goals: Explain an ADT independently of its storage representation.
Distinguish an ADT from a Java abstract class or interface.
Test returned values and observable state across a sequence.
setup: An abstract data type (ADT) describes values and operations by their behaviour. A queue stores a sequence and removes the oldest inserted item: first in, first out (FIFO). The concept does not require an array, linked nodes or a particular Java class. An implementation chooses storage while preserving that public behaviour.

worked.title: Observe a queue’s first-in, first-out rule
worked.intro:
Read the new type notation first: <String> specifies the type of elements this collection stores. In Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();, queue is the variable, the left side gives its declared type, and new ArrayDeque<>() creates an empty implementation. The empty brackets <>, called the diamond, let Java infer String from the left side. They are type notation here, not less-than/greater-than comparisons. No custom generic class is needed for these tests.

Here Deque<String> is a Java interface type and ArrayDeque<String> is a concrete implementation. We use addLast to append, removeFirst to remove the oldest item, and size/isEmpty to observe state. Strings in this example are non-null.

The public method types are void addLast(String item), String removeFirst(), int size(), and boolean isEmpty(). Call addLast as a statement; compare a removal with an expected String, a size with an int, and emptiness with a boolean assertion. The examples remove only when an item is present; testing an empty removal is deferred until exception tests.

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class QueueBehaviourTest {
    @Test void twoItems_leaveInArrivalOrder() {
        Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.addLast("A");
        queue.addLast("B");

        assertEquals(2, queue.size());
        assertEquals("A", queue.removeFirst());
        assertEquals(1, queue.size());
        assertEquals("B", queue.removeFirst());
        assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());
    }
}

steps.title: State the starting condition
steps.html: A fresh queue has no items. After appending A and then B, its abstract contents are [A, B], from oldest to newest. The test does not need access to internal storage.

steps.title: Trace each operation
steps.html:
OperationReturned itemQueue afterward
addLast("A")No return value[A]
addLast("B")No return value[A, B]
removeFirst()"A"[B]
removeFirst()"B"[]

The state before a call is part of its test input.

steps.title: Check more than the first return
steps.html: A broken implementation might return A but leave it in the queue, or forget to reduce the size. Observing the next removal and the sizes tests consequences of the operation. These assertions belong to one coherent queue sequence.

steps.title: Keep the representation abstract
steps.html: The test would express the same queue requirement for a linked implementation. It asserts arrival order and size, not a field called head or an array index chosen by the implementation.

sections.title: ADT, interface and abstract class
sections.html:
TermRole
ADTA behavioural model: values, operations and rules such as FIFO.
Java interfaceA language construct declaring operations a class can implement; it can document an ADT.
Java abstract classA class that cannot be instantiated directly and may supply state or implemented methods.
Concrete classAn instantiable implementation, such as ArrayDeque.

“Abstract” in ADT does not mean the implementation must use Java’s abstract keyword. You can test an abstract class through a concrete subclass, or an interface through a concrete implementer.

sections.title: Design state-based cases
sections.html: For a queue, try empty, one item, several items, remove until empty, and add again after draining. For a set, try adding a new member and adding a duplicate. For a stack, push A then B and expect B first. The ADT’s rule tells you which sequences distinguish it from a different or broken behaviour.

sections.title: One purpose can require several assertions
sections.html: A test method can contain several assertions when they establish one coherent behaviour. The first failing ordinary assertion stops that method, so separate unrelated scenarios into separate methods. Fresh fixtures prevent one test’s removals from silently changing another test’s starting state.

practice.title: Identify the defining behaviour
practice.prompt: You push A then B onto a stack. Which removal order tests the stack’s defining rule?

options.feedback: A stack removes the most recently pushed item first: last in, first out.
That is arrival order, characteristic of a queue.

options.text: Either order, as long as both appear
options.feedback: Stack order is part of the contract, not an unspecified detail.

practice.hint: The last item put on a stack comes off first.
practice.solution: The expected order is B then A.

practice.title: Separate abstraction from Java syntax
practice.prompt: Select the correct statements.

options.text: An ADT specifies observable behaviour without committing to a storage layout.
options.feedback: That abstraction allows different implementations of the same operations.

options.text: Every ADT must be implemented as a Java abstract class.
options.feedback: ADT is a design concept; Java classes, interfaces and implementations can represent it in different ways.

options.text: A queue test can check size after a removal.
options.feedback: Size is observable state and can reveal a missing structural update.

options.text: A passing first removal proves the queue is empty afterward.
options.feedback: Remaining contents depend on prior inserts; further observations are necessary.

practice.hint: Distinguish the behavioural concept from the language constructs.
practice.solution: The first and third statements are correct.

practice.title: Finish a state trace
practice.prompt: A fresh FIFO queue supports addLast (append), removeFirst (remove and return oldest), size and isEmpty. Trace: add A; add B; remove once; add C; remove twice. Record each returned value and the final size.
practice.hint: Keep the oldest remaining item on the left of your list.

The final size is zero and isEmpty returns true.
rubric: Removal returns A, B, C in that order.
Shows contents after each operation.
Final size is 0 with an empty queue.

practice.title: Test reuse after draining
practice.prompt:
Use Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();. The methods are void addLast(String item) (append an item), String removeFirst() (remove and return the oldest item), int size() and boolean isEmpty(). Write one JUnit method showing that after adding and removing A, you can add B and remove B. Check the intermediate and final empty states. Assume java.util.Deque and java.util.ArrayDeque are imported.

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: A reused empty structure can expose a stale head or tail in an implementation.
practice.solution:
@Test void drainedQueue_canBeUsedAgain() {
    Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.addLast("A");
    assertEquals("A", queue.removeFirst());
    assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());

    queue.addLast("B");
    assertEquals(1, queue.size());
    assertEquals("B", queue.removeFirst());
    assertTrue(queue.isEmpty());
}
rubric: Uses a fresh queue and drains A.
Adds and removes B after the empty state.
Checks values and observable empty/size state.

teachBack.prompt: What additional input does a stateful operation have besides its written arguments?
teachBack.answer: It operates on an existing object state produced by construction and earlier operations. A meaningful test must establish that state explicitly.

bridge: You can observe objects now. Next, decide whether a test needs equal values, the same object, or a particular ordering.

title: Choose equality, identity and ordering checks
summary: Match the comparison to the promise: equal contents, the identical object, or a negative/zero/positive ordering result.
goals: Distinguish object identity from value equality.
Use appropriate expectations for arrays and BigInteger results.
Test compareTo by sign unless exact values are promised.
setup: Objects create several different questions. Are these references pointing to one object? Do two objects represent equal values? Does one object sort before another? The assertion must ask the same question as the contract. A test can compile and still use the wrong notion of sameness.

worked.title: Compare strings by the promised ordering
worked.intro:
The String method int compareTo(String other) returns a negative number, zero, or a positive number for before, equal and after. Comparable is the Java interface for objects that supply a compareTo ordering operation. Its general contract promises the sign, not necessarily -1 or 1. For Strings, the ordering compares character sequences from left to right; in the one-letter example, A comes before D. The examples below intentionally use freshly constructed equal strings.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class ComparisonTest {
    @Test void equalContents_doNotRequireSameObject() {
        String left = new String("Ada");
        String right = new String("Ada");
        assertEquals(left, right);
        assertNotSame(left, right);
        assertEquals(0, left.compareTo(right));
    }

    @Test void earlierString_hasNegativeComparison() {
        assertTrue("A".compareTo("D") < 0);
    }
}

steps.title: Choose value equality
steps.html: assertEquals(left,right) checks equality using the relevant overload; for these String objects it uses String’s value equality. The character sequences are equal, so the assertion passes.

steps.title: Check identity only when it matters
steps.html: Each explicit new String creates a separate object. assertNotSame checks that distinction. A method promising to return its receiver could justify assertSame; an ordinary “equal result” promise does not.

steps.title: Test ordering by sign
steps.html: "A".compareTo("D") is negative. An expectation of exactly -1 is unnecessarily strict for the documented ordering promise. Use < 0, == 0 and > 0 for the three categories.

steps.title: Design a discriminatory pair
steps.html: If a custom comparison is documented to use only a priority, create equal priorities with different labels. Expect zero. That catches an incorrect extra tie-breaker that two identical objects would not expose.

sections.title: Build an expected value of the right type
sections.html:
import java.math.BigInteger;

BigInteger actual = BigInteger.valueOf(3).add(BigInteger.valueOf(4));
assertEquals(BigInteger.valueOf(7), actual);

Overloads are versions of a method with the same name but different parameter types; Java chooses an applicable version from the argument types. An int and a BigInteger can display the same digits without being equal objects. assertEquals(7, actual) can compile through an Object overload yet fail because Integer and BigInteger are different types. Use the expected representation promised by the API.

sections.title: Arrays need content assertions
sections.html:
int[] expected = new int[]{2, 4};
int[] actual = new int[]{2, 4};
assertArrayEquals(expected, actual);

Two separately created arrays are distinct references. Ordinary array equals does not compare element contents. For a copy contract, check equal elements and, if a distinct array is promised, also check assertNotSame. Independence after mutation may need an additional check.

sections.title: Custom objects need a stated equality rule
sections.html: To override a method is to supply a class’s own implementation of an inherited operation. A custom class that does not override equals uses the inherited Object equality rule, which checks identity. Two separately constructed objects may therefore fail assertEquals despite matching fields. Read the API. If value equality is not supplied, observe documented getters or operations rather than assuming an equality definition.

options.feedback: Any negative result satisfies the promised ordering.
This requires a specific negative value that the stated contract does not promise.
Identity does not test the ordering relation.

practice.hint: An ordering category is a sign, not necessarily a particular number.
practice.solution: Use assertTrue(a.compareTo(b) < 0).

practice.title: Match the oracle to the value
practice.prompt: Select every appropriate assertion for the stated goal.

options.feedback: The array assertion compares lengths and corresponding elements.

options.text: BigInteger result of seven: assertEquals(7, result);

teachBack.answer: Printed digits do not guarantee equal types or equality semantics. An Integer 7 and a BigInteger 7 are distinct kinds of object; construct the expected BigInteger.

bridge: So far the contract selected the cases. Next, read an implementation to find additional paths that deserve tests.

title: Trace branches and short-circuit conditions
summary: Use source code to select paths while keeping expected behaviour anchored in the contract.
goals: Distinguish statement, branch and condition coverage.
Trace which operands are actually evaluated with && and ||.
State the measured coverage denominator without treating coverage as proof.
setup:
White-box testing uses the implementation’s structure to select cases: decisions, paths and loops. The contract still determines what ought to happen. Coverage records which measured parts were exercised. It does not tell you whether the assertions were strong or whether the contract was implemented correctly.

For this lesson, a decision is the complete boolean test controlling an if or loop; an outcome is true or false. A condition is one boolean part of that decision, such as member or points >= 100. An operand is a part supplied to an operator: in A && B, A and B are operands. We will count explicitly named outcomes, so “covered” always has a stated meaning.

worked.title: A branch can be covered while a condition outcome is missed
worked.intro:
This complete class promises a bonus of 5 exactly when the caller is a member with at least 100 points; otherwise it returns 0.

class Rewards {
    static int bonus(boolean member, int points) {
        int result = 0;
        if (member && points >= 100) {
            result = 5;
        }
        return result;
    }
}

true, 100truetruetrue5
false, 100falsenot evaluatedfalse0
true, 99truefalsefalse0
@Test void memberBelowThreshold_hasNoBonus() {
    assertEquals(0, Rewards.bonus(true, 99));
}

The method above belongs in a test class with the standard JUnit 5 imports.

steps.title: Name the decision outcomes
steps.html: We count the true and false outcomes of this one if: two possible branch outcomes. The first two table rows exercise both, giving 2/2 for this explicitly defined decision measure.

steps.title: Follow short-circuit evaluation
steps.html: For A && B, Java skips B when A is false. In the second row, points ≥ 100 has a mathematical value, but the program does not evaluate it. Do not count an unexecuted operand outcome as exercised.

steps.title: Find the missing condition outcome
steps.html: Using only the first two rows, the membership operand was observed true and false, but the threshold operand was observed only true. The third row makes that operand evaluate false. For the two operands, the four tracked true/false outcomes are then all observed.

steps.title: Keep assertions independent of the branch
steps.html: The expected values 5, 0 and 0 come from the bonus contract. Executing both outcomes without checking the results would still leave a weak test. A condition accidentally changed to points > 100 would be caught by the first case.

sections.title: Three different questions about execution
sections.html:
MeasureQuestion
Statement coverageDid each measured executable statement run?
Branch coverageDid each measured decision outcome occur?
Condition coverageDid each measured atomic boolean operand evaluate both true and false?

A true-case run of this example reaches its initialization, bonus assignment and return. That does not mean the false decision outcome was exercised. Tools may count bytecode branches differently from a source-level classroom exercise; name the unit being counted.

sections.title: Short-circuit guards protect later operations
sections.html:
if (text != null && text.length() > 0) {
    return true;
}
return false;

For null, the left side is false and length() is skipped. For an empty string, both operands are evaluated and the second is false. For "A", both are true. Reversing the operand order can dereference null before the check. With ||, a true left operand skips the right operand.

sections.title: Coverage points to omissions
sections.html: Full coverage under one measure can coexist with an incorrect formula, missing input validation, or a bad assertion. The useful question is “which behaviour or structural outcome have I not challenged?” Contract classes and boundaries complement structural cases.

sections.title: Branch coverage and path coverage differ
sections.html:
A path is a sequence of outcomes through the code. Two independent if statements produce four paths in this example with no loops. Independent here means every true/false input pair is possible. The abbreviation value += 1; means value = value + 1;: read the old value, add 1, and store the result. Likewise, value += 2; adds 2. Read the complete example:

static int bits(boolean a, boolean b) {
    int value = 0;
    if (a) { value += 1; }
    if (b) { value += 2; }
    return value;
}
abExpected
falsefalse0
truefalse1
falsetrue2
truetrue3

The all-false and all-true cases cover all 4 of 4 source-level branch outcomes across two decisions, but only 2 of 4 complete paths. With n independent decisions that each have two outcomes, there can be 2ⁿ combinations. Some apparent combinations are infeasible: with tests x > 0 and x < 0 on an unchanged x, both cannot be true. Loops can create unbounded path families, so an exhaustive-path claim needs explicit bounds.

options.feedback: The value comparison null != null is false.

practice.hint: Evaluate the left operand first.
practice.solution: The left operand is false, so Java skips the right operand.

practice.title: Assess the coverage claim
practice.prompt:
For the complete Rewards.bonus code below, the suite uses only (true,100) and (false,100), with correct result assertions. Select every accurate statement. Count source-level outcomes of the single if and its two operands.

options.text: Adding (true,99) exercises the missing false threshold outcome.
options.feedback: Membership remains true, so the threshold operand is evaluated and false.

options.text: The two-case suite proves all possible rewards behaviours are correct.
options.feedback: Coverage and a small set of observations do not prove correctness for all inputs.

teachBack.prompt: Why is a skipped boolean operand not a false evaluation?
teachBack.answer: The program did not evaluate it at all. Coverage records what executed, so skipped must be distinguished from an evaluated true or false result.

bridge: Branches choose paths. Loops repeat paths, introducing empty cases, off-by-one errors and failures to make progress.

title: Test loops and explain why they stop
summary: Use empty, one-element and longer sequences to expose loop boundaries, early returns and missing progress.
goals: Trace loop initialization, condition, body and update.
Select zero-, one- and multiple-iteration cases with useful element positions.
Explain an off-by-one, early-return or nontermination defect using a concrete trace.
setup: A loop adds two questions: how many times does the body run, and does each repetition make progress? Start by locating initialization, condition, body and update. For finite arrays, empty, one-element and longer inputs expose different control-flow situations. Position matters as well as length.

worked.title: Catch a search that stops after its first element
worked.intro:
The contract promises the index of the first matching value, or -1 if no value matches. The array must be non-null. This deliberately faulty complete class is for code reading; propose a test before repairing it.

class Searches {
    static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
            if (values[i] == target) {
                return i;
            }
            return -1; // defect: stops after first non-match
        }
        return -1;
    }
}
@Test void matchAfterFirstElement_isFound() {
    int[] values = new int[]{4, 7};
    assertEquals(1, Searches.firstIndex(values, 7));
}

The @Test method goes inside a test class with the standard imports. It fails against the displayed faulty implementation.

steps.title: Choose a case that must continue
steps.html: An empty array skips the body. A match at position zero returns immediately. Neither demonstrates continuation after a non-match. [4,7] with target 7 requires a second iteration.

steps.title: Trace the first iteration
steps.html: i starts at zero. The condition 0 < 2 is true. values[0] is 4, so the equality with 7 is false. The next statement returns -1 immediately. The update i++ is never reached.

steps.title: Compare with the contract
steps.html: The contract requires index 1 because the second element is 7. The actual result is -1. The test distinguishes the intended behaviour from this early-return defect.

steps.title: Place the failure return correctly
steps.html: Return -1 only after the entire loop has found no match. Removing the inner return lets the loop advance. The final return already handles the no-match result.

sections.title: Design positions as well as lengths
sections.html:
CasePurpose
[]Zero iterations; required empty result.
[7], target 7One iteration; immediate success.
[4], target 7One iteration; no match.
[4,7,9], target 7Continuation and middle success.
[4,9,7], target 7Last valid index.
[7,4,7], target 7First occurrence rather than last.
[4,9], target 7Exhaustion without a match.

These are different behaviours, even when some calls share an expected value of -1.

sections.title: Read the boundary literally
sections.html: For length n, valid indexes are 0 through n−1. With i starting at zero, i < values.length visits those indexes. i <= values.length eventually attempts index n. On an empty array it may fail immediately. Use the smallest example that reaches the bad access.

sections.title: Identify a progress measure
sections.html:
A while (condition) loop checks the condition before each repetition and skips its body when the condition is false. Unlike the earlier for loop, this form has no separate update slot: write any update in the body. remaining--; subtracts one from remaining, just as i++; adds one to i.

The following is a method-body fragment where values is a non-null int array. A supplied helper static void process(int value) handles one element and returns normally; it does not change remaining.

int remaining = values.length;
while (remaining > 0) {
    process(values[remaining - 1]);
    // remaining-- is missing
}

For a nonempty array the condition stays true forever. A progress measure is a value you can track toward the stopping condition; here it should be the nonnegative remaining count decreasing toward zero. Add the decrement after processing an element. A timeout can bound a test run, but exceeding a time limit alone does not establish the root cause; the trace explains it. Do not execute known unbounded examples without a suitable isolated timeout.

practice.title: Expose the early return
practice.prompt:
The method promises the first matching index, or -1 if absent, for a non-null array. In the faulty implementation below, which case specifically requires continuing after a first non-match?

class Searches {
    static int firstIndex(int[] values, int target) {
        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
            if (values[i] == target) {
                return i;
            }
            return -1; // defect: stops after first non-match
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

options.feedback: The method must inspect the second item; the faulty return prevents that.
A first-item match returns before reaching the faulty line.
The body never runs, so this does not expose the early return.

practice.hint: The first element should not match, but a later element should.
practice.solution: Use [4,7] with target 7 and expected index 1.

practice.title: Spot loop defects
practice.prompt: Select every defect or justified observation.

options.text: With indexes starting at 0, i <= array.length can access one past the last element.
options.feedback: Index length is outside a Java array.

options.text: A search that returns -1 after the first non-match may skip a later match.
options.feedback: It has not checked the remainder of the sequence.

options.text: A test timing out proves the code contains an infinite loop.
options.feedback: It might also be slow, blocked or waiting. Inspect the execution to identify the cause.

options.text: Testing only a zero-length input exercises every loop-body statement.
options.feedback: An ordinary pre-test array loop skips its body for length zero.

practice.hint: Connect each claim to an actual path through the code.
practice.solution: The off-by-one and early-return observations are justified. A timeout needs diagnosis, and a zero-iteration case does not exercise the body.

practice.title: Repair an off-by-one loop
practice.prompt:
The following method promises to return the sum of all array elements, including 0 for an empty non-null array. Identify the faulty expression, describe the smallest failing input, and repair it.

static int sum(int[] values) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; i++) {
        total += values[i];
    }
    return total;
}
practice.hint: For an empty array, what is values.length and does the loop enter?
practice.solution:
With an empty array, i = 0 and length = 0, so 0 ≤ 0 enters the body and values[0] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Change the condition to i < values.length. Then the empty array skips the body and returns 0.

for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {

Uses an empty array as a concrete failing input.
Repairs the condition to <.

teachBack.prompt: What must you show to explain a nonterminating loop, beyond saying “it repeats”?
teachBack.answer: Show that the loop condition remains true and that the body/update never changes the relevant state toward termination, under the stated assumptions.

bridge: You now have many possible tests. Next, organize them so each adds useful evidence and failures point to a specific rule.

title: Build a focused test suite and justify it
summary: Combine contract classes, boundaries and code paths into a small set of well-explained tests.
goals: Link every selected test to a requirement or plausible fault.
Isolate parameter failures before combining invalid inputs.
Describe limitations and assumptions without weakening the test oracle.
setup: A test suite is a collection of tests. Its value comes from the distinct behaviours it challenges. Several tests can share a result while exposing different faults. Conversely, many tests can repeat the same ordinary case. Build a small coverage table before writing methods.

worked.title: Separate two argument restrictions
worked.intro:
Assume a public static API Bookings.reserve(int seats,String name). Contract: it returns false if seats is outside 1–4 inclusive, or name is null or empty. Otherwise it returns true. A space-only name is nonempty. There are no other restrictions. The implementation is hidden.

normal2"Ada"trueAccepted interior

steps.title: Start with a valid baseline
steps.html: (2,"Ada") is accepted. When targeting the name rule, keep seats at 2. When targeting seats, keep the name "Ada". This makes the reason for rejection identifiable.

steps.title: Add contract boundaries
steps.html: Counts 0, 1, 4 and 5 probe both edges. Counts 2 and 3 are both ordinary interior values. You can explain whether keeping both adds a particular risk check; more rows alone are not a justification.

steps.title: Avoid masked validation
steps.html: (0,null) is invalid for two reasons. A method that ignores the name completely could still reject it because seats is zero. That one case cannot establish the null-name rule. Test each restriction separately first.

steps.title: Record what the suite establishes
steps.html: This table covers each listed rule and the count endpoints. It does not exhaust all integer and String values or every possible implementation defect. A space-only name is a useful extra accepted case if trimming is a suspected accidental behaviour.

sections.title: Describe the purpose, type and assumptions
sections.html:
// Purpose: null names are rejected even with a valid seat count.
// Design: black-box; selected from the documented null-name rule.
// Assumptions: none beyond the supplied complete contract.
@Test void nullName_rejectsOtherwiseValidBooking() {
    assertFalse(Bookings.reserve(2, null),
        "A null name must be rejected when seats is valid");
}

An assumption describes context not guaranteed by the supplied specification. Do not use an assumption to contradict an explicit requirement. These are explanatory notes about the test’s context; they do not execute or change the test result.

sections.title: Think in possible faults
sections.html: Ask what change would make this test fail: using a strict rather than inclusive bound, ignoring one argument, choosing the wrong dimension, returning an incorrect constant, or failing to update state. If a supposedly wrong implementation would still pass every test, the suite may have a gap. This is a design exercise; it does not require changing production code.

sections.title: Keep failures diagnostic
sections.html: Prefer separate methods for independent invalid conditions. Use descriptive names and messages containing the expectation. Keep fixtures deterministic. A failed test is evidence to investigate: the implementation, the test expectation, or the setup may be wrong. Read the contract before changing either side.

sections.title: Use a basis, then follow definitions to uses
sections.html:
Lesson 16 traced a method with two independent if statements. Its four complete routes were false/false, true/false, false/true and true/true. Structured basis testing selects a baseline route and then routes that introduce independent control-flow alternatives. For that simple two-if example, start with false/false; change only the first decision for true/false; then change only the second for false/true. This gives a basis of three paths, while the true/true combination still remains untested. For this particular structure the count is two decisions plus one; it is not a universal test-count rule. Loops, dependent conditions and short-circuit expressions require tracing the actual possible routes. You do not need graph notation for the cases here.

Data-flow testing uses the assignment tracing from lesson 4: a definition assigns a value to a variable, and a use reads that value. Follow which assignment reaches a later read. Ask which assignment reaches the result on each path. A branch can execute while failing to update the variable later returned.

// Contract: base fee is 5; heavy parcels add 2.
static int fee(boolean heavy) {
    int result = 5;
    if (heavy) {
        int extra = 2; // computed but never used
    }
    return result;
}

For heavy=true, result is defined as 5 and never updated before return uses it. The contract expects 7. Test both false → 5 and true → 7. The explanation identifies the unused extra value and the missing update, rather than merely reporting that a branch was visited.

practice.title: Judge a suite honestly
practice.prompt: Select every sound test-design claim.

options.text: Different expected results always mean different tests are useful; identical results never are.
options.feedback: Distinct rejection conditions can share an expected result and still require separate tests.

options.text: A boundary test should name the boundary it challenges.
options.feedback: That makes the selection and expected result reviewable.

options.text: A test can pass because another invalid argument masks the missing check.
options.feedback: Combining invalid conditions can hide a defective validation path.

options.text: If all tests pass, no further reasoning about the requirements is needed.
options.feedback: Passing the selected tests does not establish untested requirements or validate a mistaken oracle.

options.text: A basis-test count is a planning aid, not proof that every feasible path or defect was checked.
options.feedback: A basis covers selected independent control-flow alternatives; additional combinations, boundaries and data-flow faults may still matter.

practice.hint: Look at the reason behind each test, not just its output.
practice.solution: Boundary justification, the masking warning, and the limited meaning of a basis-test count are sound. Coverage needs an explicit measure and cannot prove defect absence.

An empty code is a useful additional length case. The original (0,null) masks which restriction caused rejection.
rubric: At least six concrete input/expected pairs.
Separates bad level from bad code.
Includes valid endpoints and lengths on both sides of two.

practice.title: Follow a definition to its use
practice.prompt:
This complete method promises base fee 5 plus 2 for a heavy parcel. Trace which assignment reaches the return for heavy=true. Identify the root cause, write one JUnit test that exposes it, and propose a repair. Assume the method belongs to Charges and standard JUnit imports are supplied.

static int fee(boolean heavy) {
    int result = 5;
    if (heavy) {
        int extra = 2;
    }
    return result;
}

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: Which variable does return read, and is that variable changed inside the branch?
practice.solution:
result is assigned 5; the branch assigns a different local, extra; return reads the unchanged result. The heavy path returns 5 instead of 7. This is a missing update, not a failure to enter the branch.

// Purpose: the heavy surcharge affects the returned fee.
// Design: white-box data-flow case; contract supplies expected 7.
@Test void heavyParcel_includesSurcharge() {
    assertEquals(7, Charges.fee(true),
        "Heavy parcels must add 2 to the base fee of 5");
}

Replace the unused extra declaration with result += 2;. Keep a false → 5 regression case to protect the ordinary path.
rubric: Traces definition of result through the branch to its return use.
Identifies extra as unused and result as never updated.
Asserts expected 7 for heavy=true and proposes result += 2.

teachBack.prompt: Why are two separate tests for two invalid arguments often more informative than one test where both are invalid?
teachBack.answer: Each isolates a rule while the other arguments remain valid. A combined-invalid case can be rejected for one reason while the other required check is missing.

bridge: Some contracts reject invalid inputs by throwing exceptions. Next, follow that control flow before writing exception assertions.

title: Trace throw, catch and finally
summary: Follow where execution goes after an exception, and distinguish throwing an object from declaring a possible exception.
goals: Explain throw, throws, try, catch and finally in a concrete trace.
Distinguish normal return from exceptional completion.
Recognize checked exceptions and unreachable catch ordering.
setup:
An exception is an object describing an exceptional event. throw transfers control away from the current point. A matching catch can handle that event. These are language statements and blocks, not functions. Before testing an exception, be able to predict which lines execute and which lines are skipped.

In the trace, System.out.print("A "); writes A followed by a space; it does not start a new line. The letters only mark which statements ran. The try body is the attempted normal path, a matching catch is a handler, and finally contains exit work. The complete example below shows how they fit together before we trace each step.

worked.title: Follow a rejected quantity through a handler
worked.intro:
Read this complete class. Calling TraceExample.run(-1) prints the sequence below. The thrown exception is handled, so run can reach its last statement.

class TraceExample {
    static void requireNonnegative(int quantity) {
        if (quantity < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be nonnegative");
        }
    }

    static void run(int quantity) {
        try {
            System.out.print("A ");
            requireNonnegative(quantity);
            System.out.print("B ");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            System.out.print("C ");
        } finally {
            System.out.print("D ");
        }
        System.out.print("E");
    }
}
A C D E

steps.title: Start in the try block
steps.html: A prints. The call receives -1, so quantity < 0 is true. new IllegalArgumentException(...) creates the exception object; throw throws it.

steps.title: Skip the remaining normal path
steps.html: requireNonnegative does not return normally. Control does not continue to B. It searches for a matching handler, which is the surrounding catch for IllegalArgumentException.

steps.title: Run the matching catch
steps.html: The variable ex refers to the thrown object. C prints. This handler finishes normally and does not rethrow, so execution can continue after the try statement.

steps.title: Run finally before continuing
steps.html: D prints as control leaves the try/catch, then E prints. For an accepted quantity, the sequence is A B D E. A finally block runs on ordinary and exceptional exits when execution reaches that exit; abrupt JVM termination is outside that normal guarantee.

sections.title: Five pieces with different jobs
sections.html:
SyntaxMeaning
try { ... }Run code whose exceptions may be handled here.
throw new SomeException(...)Throw a particular exception object now.
catch (SomeException ex) { ... }Handle a matching thrown exception using variable ex.
throws IOExceptionDeclare that a method may propagate that exception; does not throw by itself.
finally { ... }Perform exit work whether the try completed normally or exceptionally.

A method’s return type describes normal results. An int method may throw instead of returning an int. It still cannot return null as an int value.

sections.title: Checked and unchecked exceptions
sections.html:
A subclass is a more specific kind of class, also called a subtype. IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException are kinds of RuntimeException; RuntimeException and IOException are kinds of Exception. An exception can therefore match a handler for its own type or a more general parent type.

For a checked exception such as IOException, calling code generally must catch it or declare it with throws. RuntimeException subclasses, including IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException, are unchecked: the compiler does not require that catch-or-declare step. They can still be documented, thrown, caught and tested.

sections.title: Catch order and propagation
sections.html: Handlers are tried in order. A broad catch (Exception ex) before catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) makes the latter unreachable and causes a compilation error. Put a more specific handler first when both are needed. If no handler matches, the exception propagates outward after any applicable finally block. Do not return from finally merely to hide the failure; it can replace a pending return or exception.

practice.title: Predict the accepted path
practice.prompt:
For the complete TraceExample class below, what prints when run(0) is called?

class TraceExample {
    static void requireNonnegative(int quantity) {
        if (quantity < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("quantity must be nonnegative");
        }
    }

    static void run(int quantity) {
        try {
            System.out.print("A ");
            requireNonnegative(quantity);
            System.out.print("B ");
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            System.out.print("C ");
        } finally {
            System.out.print("D ");
        }
        System.out.print("E");
    }
}

options.feedback: The check returns normally, B runs, catch is skipped, and finally runs before E.
The catch path is used for a negative quantity, not zero.
The finally block also runs on the normal path.
A catch block does not run just because a try block finishes.

practice.hint: Zero satisfies the nonnegative check.
practice.solution: The sequence is A B D E.

practice.title: Read exception syntax correctly
practice.prompt: Select every correct statement.

options.text: A throws declaration does not itself throw an exception.
options.feedback: It declares possible propagation; an executed throw or failing operation causes the event.

options.text: An int-returning method may complete by throwing an exception instead of returning a number.
options.feedback: Normal and exceptional completion are different control-flow outcomes.

options.text: catch (Exception e) before catch (IllegalArgumentException e) is valid ordering.
options.feedback: The broad first catch already handles that subtype, making the later catch unreachable.

options.text: Code immediately after a throwing call in the same try block always runs.
options.feedback: An exception skips the remaining normal statements in that try path.

practice.hint: Separate syntax declarations from runtime control flow.
practice.solution: The throws distinction and exceptional completion of an int method are correct.

practice.title: Trace a rethrow
practice.prompt:
The snippet is the body of static void trace(boolean bad). Trace the prints for trace(true). Assume the caller does not catch the exception. Does Z print?

try {
    System.out.print("W ");
    if (bad) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad");
    }
} catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
    System.out.print("X ");
    throw ex;
} finally {
    System.out.print("Y ");
}
System.out.print("Z");
practice.hint: A catch block can handle an exception by rethrowing it, so it need not complete normally.
practice.solution: For trace(true), W, X and Y print in that order. The same exception propagates from catch after finally executes. Z is not reached on this execution path. The code can compile because the method also has a normal path when bad is false; that path prints W Y Z.
rubric: Print sequence is W X Y.
Explains rethrow and finally.
States Z is skipped because the exception propagates.

practice.title: Distinguish declaration and handling
practice.prompt: Assume Loader provides static String read() throws java.io.IOException. Write one wrapper method that catches IOException and returns "unavailable", and another wrapper that lets the same checked exception propagate. Do not throw a new exception merely because the signature uses throws.
practice.hint: The propagating wrapper needs a throws clause; the handling wrapper needs a catch block.
practice.solution:
static String readOrFallback() {
    try {
        return Loader.read();
    } catch (java.io.IOException ex) {
        return "unavailable";
    }
}

static String readOrPropagate() throws java.io.IOException {
    return Loader.read();
}

The fallback is a chosen wrapper policy. A real caller should choose a fallback only when it is meaningful for that application.
rubric: Catches exactly IOException in the handling wrapper.
Declares IOException on the propagating wrapper.
Preserves the normal String return and does not invent an extra throw.

teachBack.prompt: When a method throws, what happens to the statement after its call?
teachBack.answer: It is skipped on that exceptional path until a handler transfers control elsewhere. If an enclosing handler finishes normally, execution continues after that try/catch statement, not by returning to the skipped line.

bridge: Now express “this exact call must throw this kind of exception” as a JUnit assertion.

title: Write precise exception tests
summary: Use assertThrows with a deferred call, inspect the returned exception, and keep setup outside the asserted operation.
goals: Write assertThrows with a class literal and an executable lambda.
Check a documented exception message separately from JUnit’s failure message.
Avoid a false positive caused by a different operation throwing.
setup: An exception test succeeds when the required exceptional behaviour occurs. JUnit must run the target operation itself so it can observe the outcome. A lambda such as () -> Limits.requirePositive(0) supplies that operation for later execution. It does not call the method before assertThrows starts.

worked.title: Check the type and the documented message
worked.intro:
This complete implementation promises IllegalArgumentException with the exact message shown for nonpositive values. The test is a separate class in the same package.

class Limits {
    static void requirePositive(int amount) {
        if (amount <= 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
        }
    }
}
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class LimitsTest {
    @Test void zeroAmount_isRejectedWithDocumentedMessage() {
        IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(
            IllegalArgumentException.class,
            () -> Limits.requirePositive(0),
            "Zero must be rejected");

        assertEquals("amount must be positive", ex.getMessage());
    }
}

steps.title: Pass the exception class
steps.html: IllegalArgumentException.class identifies the expected type. It is a class literal, not a constructed exception and not a quoted string.

steps.title: Defer the single operation
steps.html: () -> Limits.requirePositive(0) is a zero-argument lambda. JUnit executes its body. Writing the method call directly in that argument position would not provide the required executable callback.

steps.title: Understand the three outcomes
steps.html: If no exception is thrown, assertThrows fails. If the thrown type is incompatible, it fails. If the expected type or a subtype is thrown, it passes and returns that exception object. Here the result is stored in ex.

steps.title: Check the message separately
steps.html: The final argument "Zero must be rejected" is JUnit’s diagnostic if its assertion fails. It is not the expected exception message. The separate assertEquals compares the exact contract message with ex.getMessage().

sections.title: Keep construction outside the lambda
sections.html:
For this separate API, Service(int limit) creates a service for a nonnegative limit and throws IllegalArgumentException for a negative limit. void setLimit(int limit) likewise rejects negatives with IllegalArgumentException. The integer 0 is a valid constructor argument.

Service service = new Service(0);
assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
    () -> service.setLimit(-1));

If you put both the constructor and setLimit inside the lambda, a constructor exception of the expected type could satisfy the test before setLimit runs. Arrange valid state first and put only the operation being checked inside assertThrows. Match the asserted exception type to the contract; Exception.class is often too broad.

A one-operation lambda uses () -> call(). A block lambda uses () -> { statement; statement; }; its braces contain statements run later by JUnit. Both defer execution. A larger block also creates more possible places for an exception to arise, so keep this exception test’s block limited to the intended action.

sections.title: Subtype acceptance and exact types
sections.html: assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, ...) also accepts a subclass such as NumberFormatException. That follows the type relationship. If a contract truly requires the exact class, JUnit 5 supplies assertThrowsExactly. Most tests should follow what the contract promises, rather than assuming “exact” is always better.

sections.title: Check acceptance too
sections.html: A method that throws for every input could pass only-rejection tests. Add a valid boundary or ordinary case. Use assertDoesNotThrow(() -> ...) when absence of an exception is the observation; also assert returned values or state if the contract promises them. For a void operation, inspect the relevant state after the call when possible.

practice.title: Choose the valid exception assertion
practice.prompt: Assume Limits provides the static method void requirePositive(int amount), which rejects zero with IllegalArgumentException. Which assertion has the correct shape?

options.feedback: It supplies the exception class and defers the target operation.
A void method call is not the executable callback required by assertThrows.
A void call has no boolean result, and this does not assert an exception.
A void call has no value to compare; rejection is an exceptional outcome.

practice.hint: JUnit needs a callback that it can execute.
practice.solution: Use assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> Limits.requirePositive(0)).

practice.title: Understand what the test proves
practice.prompt: Assume action is a valid zero-argument executable callback and the standard JUnit assertion imports are present. Select every correct statement about assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, action, "must reject").

options.text: The text "must reject" is JUnit’s failure message.
options.feedback: It explains an assertion failure, rather than matching the thrown message.

options.text: The assertion returns the exception if the expected type is thrown.
options.feedback: You can then inspect its documented properties.

options.text: A NumberFormatException satisfies the expected type.
options.feedback: NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException.

options.text: The assertion passes if action returns normally.
options.feedback: Normal completion means no required exception occurred.

practice.hint: Distinguish the asserted type, returned object and diagnostic message.
practice.solution: The first three statements are correct. Normal completion makes assertThrows fail.

practice.title: Repair the wrong observation
practice.prompt:
The API Counter(int initial) accepts nonnegative initial values and rejects negative initial values with IllegalArgumentException. void set(int value) rejects negatives with IllegalArgumentException. Repair this test so it actually checks set, and explain the problem.

@Test void rejectsNegativeSet() {
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> {
        Counter counter = new Counter(-1);
        counter.set(-2);
    });
}

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: Build a valid counter before JUnit begins observing the target operation.
practice.solution:
@Test void rejectsNegativeSet() {
    Counter counter = new Counter(0);
    assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class,
        () -> counter.set(-2));
}

The original may pass because the constructor rejects -1, so set is never called. Valid construction outside the lambda removes that false positive.
rubric: Constructs a valid object outside the lambda.
Lambda contains the targeted set call.
Explains that a constructor exception could satisfy the original assertion.

practice.title: Write a complete rejection and acceptance pair
practice.prompt:
Assume Counter(int initial) creates a counter with the supplied nonnegative value, int get() reads it, and void set(int value) accepts zero or positive values. A negative set must throw IllegalArgumentException with exact message "value must be nonnegative" and leave the counter unchanged. Write two @Test methods: negative set, and accepted zero. Imports are supplied.

Use JUnit 5: assume org.junit.jupiter.api.Test and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* are imported. Write the methods inside a nonprivate test class in the same package as the API.
practice.hint: Check the rejection’s type, message and state; then use a fresh counter for the valid boundary.
practice.solution:
@Test void negativeSet_rejectsAndPreservesState() {
    Counter counter = new Counter(4);
    IllegalArgumentException ex = assertThrows(
        IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> counter.set(-1));
    assertEquals("value must be nonnegative", ex.getMessage());
    assertEquals(4, counter.get());
}

@Test void zeroSet_isAccepted() {
    Counter counter = new Counter(4);
    assertDoesNotThrow(() -> counter.set(0));
    assertEquals(0, counter.get());
}
rubric: Asserts IllegalArgumentException using a lambda for set(-1).
Checks the exact documented message and unchanged value 4.
Uses a separate fresh fixture to check zero is accepted and stored.

teachBack.prompt: Why does an exception test need the target call inside a lambda?
teachBack.answer: The lambda lets JUnit invoke the operation while observing it. If the call happens before the assertion receives it, JUnit cannot use that assertion to check its exception.

bridge: Next, read and repair manual try/catch tests, then apply the same contract discipline to defensive code and defect reports.
